title: Cervical vertebrae (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender, with surface detail added by an image model.

rows: Location
First cervical vertebra, a ring of bone at the top of the vertebral column that carries the skull.
Articulates with

Occipital condyles of the skull above, at the atlanto-occipital joints (nodding the head). Axis below, at a lateral atlantoaxial joint on each side and at the median joint between its anterior arch and the dens (turning the head).
Features

It has no body and no spinous process. Two lateral masses are joined by an anterior and a posterior arch. A groove on the upper surface of the posterior arch carries the vertebral artery and the first cervical nerve. The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against the anterior arch.
hy: Jefferson fracture: a heavy load on the top of the head, as in diving into shallow water, squeezes the atlas between the skull and the axis and can burst the ring, breaking its anterior and posterior arches. The ring widens, so the spinal cord is often spared.

In rheumatoid arthritis and in Down syndrome the transverse ligament can be weak or lax. The atlas can then slide forward on the axis (atlantoaxial subluxation) and the dens can press on the spinal cord.

rows: Location
Second cervical vertebra. It is the pivot on which the atlas and the skull turn.
Articulates with
Atlas above, by the dens, which meets the anterior arch of the atlas, and by a facet on each side for the lateral mass. Third cervical vertebra below.
Features

The dens (odontoid process) projects up from its body. It has a large bifid spinous process and a transverse foramen in each transverse process. The alar ligaments run from the dens to the skull at the sides of the foramen magnum and limit rotation of the head.
hy: Hangman fracture: sudden hyperextension of the head, as in hanging or when the chin strikes the dashboard in a car crash, breaks the arch of the axis on both sides between its upper and lower articular processes (pars interarticularis). The body of the axis can then slide forward on C3.
A fracture of the dens usually runs through its base and often fails to unite, partly because the broken piece can lose its blood supply.

rows: Location
The third to sixth vertebrae of the neck, between the axis above and C7 below.
Features

Small, wide body whose upper side edges turn up as the uncinate processes. Large triangular vertebral foramen. A transverse foramen in each transverse process for the vertebral artery and veins. Short spinous process, usually bifid. The anterior tubercle of the transverse process of C6 is large and is called the carotid tubercle, because the common carotid artery can be pressed against it.
hy: Cervical discs herniate most often between C5 and C6 and between C6 and C7, and usually press on the nerve root that leaves at that level: C6 and C7, respectively.

rows: Location
Seventh and lowest cervical vertebra, at the junction of the neck and the thorax.
Articulates with
Sixth cervical vertebra above and first thoracic vertebra below.
Features

Long spinous process that is not bifid and is usually the most prominent one at the base of the neck, which makes it a landmark for counting vertebrae. Its transverse foramina are small: the vertebral artery usually does not pass through them but enters at C6.
hy: A cervical rib, an extra rib attached to C7 in about 1 in 100 people, can press on the lower trunk of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery (thoracic outlet syndrome), causing pain and numbness along the inner side of the forearm and hand, wasting of the small hand muscles, and sometimes a weak pulse.

rows: Location
First of the twelve thoracic vertebrae, just below C7.
Articulates with

C7 above and T2 below. On each side the head of the first rib meets its body and the tubercle of the first rib meets its transverse process. The head of the second rib meets the lower edge of its body and the upper edge of the body of T2.
Features

On each side of the body there is a whole facet above for the first rib and a demifacet below for the second, where a typical thoracic vertebra has two demifacets. Its long, nearly horizontal spinous process can be as prominent as that of C7.
hy: Spinal nerves C1 to C7 leave above the vertebra of the same number, and C8 leaves between C7 and T1. From T1 down, each nerve leaves below its own vertebra.

rows: Location
Between the bodies of neighboring vertebrae from C2 and C3 down to L5 and S1. There is none between the atlas and the axis.
Parts
An outer ring of fibrocartilage, the anulus fibrosus, around a gel-like center, the nucleus pulposus.
Function
Bear weight, absorb shock, and allow movement between the vertebrae.
hy: In a herniated disc the nucleus pulposus bulges through the anulus, usually posterolaterally. It is most common at L4 to L5 and L5 to S1 and usually compresses the nerve root numbered for the vertebra below (L5 at an L4 to L5 disc).
The nucleus pulposus is a remnant of the notochord.

rows: Location
Highest rib, at the root of the neck under the clavicle, where it borders the superior thoracic aperture. It is the broadest and most sharply curved rib and the shortest of the true ribs.
Articulates with
Body of T1 only, by a single facet on its head. Transverse process of T1, by its tubercle. Manubrium of the sternum, through the first costal cartilage.
Features

Flat, with an upper and a lower surface. On the upper surface the scalene tubercle, for the anterior scalene muscle, lies between two grooves: one in front for the subclavian vein and one behind for the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus.
hy: A tumor at the apex of the lung (Pancoast tumor) can invade the first rib, the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, and the sympathetic trunk, causing pain in the shoulder and along the inner side of the arm, wasting of the small hand muscles, and Horner syndrome.
